title: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We have reason to believe that species in a state of nature are limited in their ranges by the competition of other organic beings quite as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Acclimatisation.”. Scope: plants and animals in nature

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Broad occurrence, climate and interaction resources support comparative variance-partitioning. Observational correlations and missing interactions prevent a decisive global causal comparison.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Partition explained variation in range limits between climate and biotic-interaction predictors across many species, supplemented by transplants or invasions beyond native boundaries. A median biotic contribution at least as large as climate supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Climate and competitors covary spatially.

Interaction databases omit many weak, local or context-dependent interactions.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.42
analysis feasibility: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.64
data adequacy: 0.59
data existence: 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The relative frequency of climatic and biotic boundaries is a definable ratio, and the same public climate, occurrence, and tolerance sources support it. Coverage of physiological limits restricts the ratio to a subset of taxa, mostly terrestrial ectotherms. Even there, turnover and failed dispersal mimic competition, so the test is informative with a serious confound rather than decisive for the full biota.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify range boundaries as coinciding with physiological climate limits or as lying inside those limits where interacting species turn over, then compare the two frequencies. The claim would be confirmed if biotic boundaries are at least as common as climatic ones; it would be refuted if most boundaries match tolerance limits and competitor turnover adds no explanatory power.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Dispersal limitation produces interior edges that look biotic.

Species turnover at an edge is a proxy for competition, not a demonstration of it.

Tolerance data exist for a minority of species, so many boundaries cannot be classified.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.58
data existence: 0.74
operationalizability: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.46
